title: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
description: Image caption, The governor of Jawzjan province, Abdullah Sarhadi, who fought for the Taliban was held in US detention in Guantanamo Bay for several y
body: Image caption, The governor of Jawzjan province, Abdullah Sarhadi, who fought for the Taliban was held in US detention in Guantanamo Bay for several years ByKawoon KhamooshBBC World ServiceReporting fromSheberghan, Kabul and KandaharGovernor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque - then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds.A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings.She will not take no for an answer.In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses."If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn't be here… I have taken my decision," she says.After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are "mindless" and "deficient in intellect", to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him.The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban's rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021.Figure caption, Watch: Eighteen-year-old woman argues her case for a divorce, saying her "honour and dignity have already been ruined"In that time, women have been excluded from most workplaces, banned from universities and may not travel alone or visit parks and leisure centres.In encounters spread over two years, the BBC gained unusual access to influential figures in the extreme Islamist movement, spending time with men who once planned suicide attacks or spent years in underground hideouts, but are now officials and soldiers.The Taliban came into power saying they had changed, but many of their policies are similar to the hard-line interpretation of Sharia - Islamic religious law - they imposed in the 1990s.The men we met seemed to want to present themselves as reasonable, yet were not keen to discuss their past violence. And we saw moments of unease between the rulers and those they rule.Governor Sarhadi says Tuba – not her real name – should stay in the marriage."Ask yourself: 'Who would marry me after I get my divorce?'" says Sarhadi. "You'll have to compromise a lot or you'll lose your dignity and honour.""Mr Governor, my honour and dignity have already been ruined," she responds.Her husband listens, awaiting his turn to speak.Under Sharia, a woman requesting that her husband agrees to a divorce may have to return some or all of the money given to her by him when they married. A financial settlement is often agreed. But this woman's husband says he wants four times the amount, which her family refuses to pay.The governor says the woman should be given her own room. He adds that officials will warn him not to beat her - "otherwise he'd be jailed".Unsatisfied, Tuba's father later tells the BBC the family will pursue divorce through the courts, even though, under the Taliban's court system, it is very difficult for a woman to get a divorce without the husband's consent.Image source, EPA/REX/ShutterstockImage caption, A hole left by the destruction of one of the Buddha statues in Bamiyan -  Sarhadi says he destroyed itSarhadi was a military commander during the Taliban's first stint in power in the 1990s. He was among thousands of insurgents who surrendered in late 2001 as a US-led coalition ousted the group.He was held for several years in US detention in Guantanamo Bay, but eventually released.When the Taliban regained power, he became a governor - first in the province of Bamiyan, then when we met him in late June, in Sheberghan city in Jawzjan province. He has recently become deputy commander of a military corps in the northern province of Kunduz.Tapping on an old-style mobile with a tiny screen, he says a recent ban on smartphones for officials has slowed things down. "Before, you could send a quick message… sending documents and getting an answer fast." If he says any more about the ban, "it will cause trouble", he adds.But in other ways his worldview seems largely unchanged from the Taliban's position 25 years ago. Then, he was a military commander in Bamiyan, where the Taliban blew up ancient giant Buddha statues, triggering international shock and condemnation.He initially tries to avoid our questions about the archaeological site, but eventually, he says: "I destroyed it with my own hands."Whatever we did and we do is in accordance with the guidance and God's law… We smash idols rather than sell them. Why should I regret? It was God's will."In the capital Kabul, we meet another senior Taliban figure who swapped a violent past for a role with the ruling administration.Habibullah Badr drives us through the streets in an armoured car.He says he was previously "responsible for the operations of suicide attackers" in Kabul."I know all the roads and streets very well… we had all the information we needed about Kabul and its alleys," he says. "There were areas that needed a long time to plan."Taliban suicide attacks killed thousands of people in Afghanistan, including many civilians.Badr is cautious about discussing his past though, fearing it will "make people upset" and could "reopen wounds".Asked about civilian deaths, he says the Taliban targeted US convoys and that civilians were urged to stay away from foreign bases.Whenever I try to ask him about specific attacks that took place in civilian areas, he evades the question.Image caption, Habibullah Badr says that in the past he was involved in operations involving suicide attacksHe is currently taking time out from official roles for medical treatment, but was previously deputy head of prisons for the whole country – and ran the very jail where he was held on death row under the previous government.Badr invites us to join him at a tribal gathering, where the head of a charitable foundation is to honour him with a medal. But things take an unexpected turn."Mr Badr is a pride for Afghanistan and a great fighter," says Sultan Mohammad Talaee. "But I also have a complaint. If the schools and education were open to all it would be a great work for Afghanistan. I hope this doesn't offend you."An awkward silence follows, his audience unsure how to react. Talaee's microphone is swiftly removed.Afterwards, he tells the BBC: "I requested for the girls' schools to reopen… seeking knowledge is an obligation for both men and women in Islam."He adds: "There were other things I wanted to say but they didn't let me talk more."Often those who speak out face much more severe consequences.Women told us of the deep despair they felt over dreams thwarted by restrictions on education, and of friends jailed for protesting.Most journalists we spoke to said they had been summoned or questioned by the Taliban's intelligence organisation, Estikhbaraat.The BBC put some of these concerns to the Taliban government's spokesman, known as Zabihullah Mujahid.Image caption, Zabihullah Mujahid says women's rights and freedom of speech need to be seen "through the Sharia lens"He has been a public face for the Taliban government since 2021. He still uses the pseudonym he went by for years during the insurgency, but he told us his real name is Tahir Shah Seddiqi - revealing it publicly for the first time.In a lavish press centre funded by the Americans for the previous government, we ask him about the first press conference he gave there, two days after the Taliban took control of the country.Then, he told the world the Taliban government would allow women to work and study "within our frameworks" and they would "be very active" in society. Why did they fail to keep their word?"We are committed to women's rights, freedom of speech and other things within Sharia," he replies. "We should see everything through the Sharia lens."Allowing women to work in offices such as his own "would lead to immoralities" and "their dignity would be undermined", he adds.He says the issue of education for women is "under discussions… we need a Sharia-based solution for it".When questioned about the Taliban's crackdown on media freedom, he says: "In a society like Afghanistan we have our restrictions. We can't let media do whatever propaganda they want… they can't broadcast against Islamic laws and rites."The Taliban government sits in Kabul, but Mujahid spends a lot of time in the southern city of Kandahar, the Taliban's heartland, which some now consider the de facto capital.We ask to meet the Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, who is based there. He rarely appears in public and has never given a media interview - we are told it will not be possible at the moment.Restrictions have been tightened in Kandahar since I last visited two years ago. Now men must have beards. Radio stations are not allowed to play music or broadcast women's voices, and we were not allowed to film in the city.Two hours' drive away, along dusty roads, some of the group's most devoted former fighters showed the BBC the insurgents' old secret cave network.Abid Lalai, a former fighter who now mans a checkpoint as part of a security force under the interior ministry, shows us the holes he fired from and the places he used to put his Quran and hang AK-47s.Image caption, Abid Lalai is one of many Taliban fighters who hid out in caves to evade capture under previous governmentsHis superior, Abdul Samad, shows us an unmarked graveyard, saying his father is buried here, killed fighting for the Taliban.The area is one of the most deprived in a country where the UN says three in four people cannot provide for their basic needs. Samad says the local population desperately need water, roads and clinics."Emirate [Taliban] officials have not forgotten us," says Samad. He says the leaders may be busy with other priorities. "We are hopeful, they will look after us sometime."Five years since the Taliban began their second stint in power, poverty, unemployment and economic instability remain pressing concerns.Taliban figures we spoke to said they were working to tackle them, but we met other people who believe the group itself is the country's main problem."I'm speechless about how a group that has no understanding about life is suddenly in power," says Hoda - not her real name - a woman who protested on the streets when the Taliban first returned to power."Women can't accept this situation," she tells the BBC. "They might advance restrictions but it won't stay like this forever.""I think the Taliban are scared of educated women," she adds. "That's why they restrict women. They want uneducated women so they can't raise wise men. Because that would end the Taliban."Additional reporting by Hafizullah Maroof

schema.headline: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan

title: 'I didn't speak the Queen's English': Why people worry about their accents
description: Growing up in Manchester, Mia Tanswell didn't give her accent much thought - until her first week at university in Loughborough."I knew people were go
body: Growing up in Manchester, Mia Tanswell didn't give her accent much thought - until her first week at university in Loughborough."I knew people were going to notice that I was northern and that I didn't speak the 'Queen's English'," the 22-year-old says."Definitely in seminars I would sometimes feel like my accent would sound a bit less intellectual than other people, especially if I was the only northern student in the classroom."She's not alone. Fresh polling seen by the BBC suggests many workers still see so-called "accent bias" as a problem.The survey found one in 10 people in Britain feel anxious or self-conscious about their accent in high stakes professional settings such as speaking up in a business meeting.The research, conducted by the organisation More in Common of more than 3,300 adults across England, Scotland and Wales, found accent-related anxiety in work settings like these was highest among Geordies - from the region around Newcastle - and those with an east London - or Cockney - accent (at 19%), followed by people with a Welsh accent (at 18%).Around 5% of respondents believed their accent had cost them a promotion, pay rise or senior role. "Brummies" - people from Birmingham - were the most likely to feel this, at 13%.Respondents with a West Country accent reported the highest rate of having their accent mocked or criticised by colleagues, at 15%, followed by 13% of those with a Geordie accent.The poll was commissioned by Common Ground, an organisation which aims to promote social cohesion. Its founder, Lara Newman, has worked in construction, property and the built environment industry for more than 30 years, and says she changed her own accent to get ahead in the workplace."I am incredibly realistic about what would have happened had I gone to university or gone into the workplace with a strong west country accent," she says. "I felt like that was going to be an issue for me."Common Ground aims to support people from disadvantaged backgrounds into work but she says one of the layers creating a barrier to them is accent."I think there is a problem in the sense that [an accent] implies a level of education or otherwise. It implies class," she says.Most employers would say that is at least their ambition, to treat applicants and employees equally, regardless of their accent. Charlotte Davies, career expert at LinkedIn, says while there is still progress to be made "the direction of travel is encouraging"."Hiring is increasingly about skills, not background or polish. "Your accent is part of your story, and the workplaces getting this right, treat that as a strength, not something to smooth out," she says.Sian Jackson, a partner at law firm Mills & Reeve, says her company has recently changed its approach to encourage more local hiring and a diversity of accents."We don't judge, we scrutinise based on capability beyond somebody's accent, or appearance. Like any other prejudice or bias it's about being conscious of it so you can then set it aside," she says."We feel we've come a long way as a firm, but we are behind nationally compared to things like gender, so there is more progress to be made on accents."

schema.headline: 'I didn't speak the Queen's English': Why people worry about their accents

title: Shein aims for almost $27bn valuation in stock market debut
description: Fast-fashion giant Shein could see its stock market valuation reach almost $27bn (£19.8bn) when its makes its debut in Hong Kong on 1 September.The lo
body: Fast-fashion giant Shein could see its stock market valuation reach almost $27bn (£19.8bn) when its makes its debut in Hong Kong on 1 September.The long-awaited move comes after failed attempts to list in the US and London due to regulatory challenges amid scrutiny of the firm, which has its headquarters in Singapore but was founded in China.Since it was founded in 2008, Shein has risen to become one of the world's biggest fast-fashion retailers, with customers in more than 150 countries.The e-commerce giant is known for selling ultra-cheap clothes, backed by a vast network of factories in China that are able to quickly manufacture new products based on the latest trends.Shein said in a filing on Monday, external that it will offer nearly 280 million shares for between HK$47.60 ($6.07; £4.45) and HK$49.50 each.At the top of the range, the share sale would raise $1.77bn (£1.3bn) for the company and give it a market valuation of $26.8bn.But that is much lower than the $100bn it was worth in 2022, reflecting weaker sales growth and higher costs.The initial public offering (IPO) is being backed by Wall Street investment giants Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JP Morgan.The company will make its highly anticipated debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange after efforts to go public since 2023.Hong Kong has been revived as "one of the largest IPO markets" after attracting more firms from mainland China, said economics associate professor Feng Qu from the Nanyang Technological University.Shein is likely to command a higher valuation in Hong Kong than it would in London, where regulatory scrutiny derailed its plans to sell shares there, Feng said.Chinese companies may also be wary of selling shares in the US as tensions between the world's two largest economies could result in firms being de-listed, he added.The company also said the Iran war had hit demand, increased costs and caused delays of deliveries in some markets.The first-quarter figures also partly reflected a paper loss of $328m due to an accounting change for special investor shares. The shares can be turned into ordinary stock later, and their value can change before a listing.Some investors are questioning whether higher costs and regulatory challenges will affect Shein's ability to get goods swiftly and cheaply to market.Marguerite LeRolland from market research company Euromonitor International told the BBC that the firm's sales have slowed in the US partly due to the end of the de minimis exemption.The exemption helped retailers like Shein and its fierce rival Temu grow quickly in the US as they were able to deliver goods without incurring import taxes.These factors could "narrow the price gap" between Shein and competitors like Primark and H&M, she added.Jane Foley, Rabobank's head of FX strategy, told the BBC's Today programme that the ending of the de minimis exemption "really did undermine the core business model of Shein", adding that the EU has done something similar.Richard Lim of research firm Retail Economics said Chinese retail giants such as Shein have caused "a huge wave of destruction" in markets like the UK, with more established companies struggling to compete.The British retail industry believes Shein is "not playing on a level playing field", he told the BBC.It is expected that the UK will impose similar restrictions as the US and EU on small packages from Chinese retailers in 2028.

schema.headline: Shein aims for almost $27bn valuation in stock market debut

title: Esports: How to get £2,000 to play computer games at university
description: Dray encouraged students to make use of every scholarship, bursary and opportunity available to them.He said: "Many of these funds are available to mo
body: Dray encouraged students to make use of every scholarship, bursary and opportunity available to them.He said: "Many of these funds are available to more students than they realise, and everyone should be taking full advantage."The average graduate in England leaves university with debts of more than £47,500. Scholarships such as Roehampton's can reduce student debt and provide additional financial support.Thomas Cole, an esports player nicknamed Pac who specialises in the racing game Trackmania, said universities offering unique scholarships, including esports, encourages students academically by reducing the level of financial stress they might face.  "Uni students being paid to play a game alongside doing their studies, it's definitely cracking. If I had gone to uni, I would have loved that," he says."If it doesn't let the academic side suffer, then I think being offered something like that really spurs on people to be better in gaming," he says.Tom Allingham, student money expert from the Save the Student personal finance site, regularly advises incoming first years to seek out scholarships and learn more about what their university offers. "Unfortunately, I don't think there is enough awareness on scholarships," he said. "There is a lot of funding that goes unclaimed because students don't know that they're eligible for it," he added.Save the Student helps share various scholarships and bursaries on their website. "What we try to get across is you can get extra funding for so many different reasons."

schema.headline: Esports: How to get £2,000 to play computer games at university

title: Yr Wyddfa rows between people queuing and those skipping the line
description: Visitors to Wales' highest mountain are being urged to respect others by not skipping queues to reach the top following rows among climbers.Recent hot
body: Visitors to Wales' highest mountain are being urged to respect others by not skipping queues to reach the top following rows among climbers.Recent hot weather means there have been bumper summer crowds at Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, where people have reportedly waited more than one hour to reach the 1,085m (3,560ft)-high summit.Social media videos have shown arguments among queue-jumpers and those patiently waiting their turn to touch the metal plate that marks the top.A recent video showed Marc Screeton, from Manchester, being heckled as he bypassed the line, saying: "Imagine queuing on a mountain? No chance."But others have said queuing is necessary for safety reasons.The mountain's growing popularity in Eryri National Park, also known as Snowdonia, has led to bottlenecks, and queues are now common on the stone steps leading to a metal plate or trig point where people pose for photos and videos.Speaking to BBC Wales, walkers on the mountain had mixed views about those jumping the queues. Lucy Taylor said: "I think you should queue because it's really quite dangerous and everyone's trying to get up there - it's just not safe."

schema.headline: Yr Wyddfa rows between people queuing and those skipping the line

title: Vietnam: Gen Z seek justice for teen killed in ex-politician's car crash
description: Until recently, there would have been little to distinguish Vietnam's so-called Justice Tree from the hundreds of others lining the streets of Hanoi.
body: Until recently, there would have been little to distinguish Vietnam's so-called Justice Tree from the hundreds of others lining the streets of Hanoi. Then the bouquets started piling up.It was here that former politician Nguyen Sy Cuong was driving his BMW in May last year when he veered into the opposite lane and smashed into a motorbike carrying a father and his teenage daughter.The father, Do Viet Hung, suffered a broken leg but survived. The daughter, 18-year-old Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy, died in hospital 10 days after the collision, which severed her right leg.Fifteen months later, her death and the silence surrounding it has become a lightning rod for discontent among Vietnam's youth.In early August, a legion of anonymous social media users started publishing millions of posts with the hashtags #NguyenSyCuong and #BMW across Facebook, Instagram, Threads and X. The users identified themselves as Gen Z – and they demanded accountability.Initial discussions circled around whether the former politician was in fact the one who had caused the accident, and why authorities had only released sparse information.Some pointed to reports that the driver of the BMW had the initials NSC and was born in 1961, leading to speculation that he was a former member of parliament. Others claimed the incident had been swept under the rug due to the influence of powerful figures. Many reported that their posts had been deleted by social media platforms at the request of the Vietnamese government – providing screenshots of notifications as evidence. These claims could not be independently verified.Expressions of outrage and calls for a proper investigation grew in number, volume and force.Meanwhile, masked flower bearers started to appear, gravitating towards the scene of the incident and laying vibrant bouquets at the base of what has now been dubbed the Justice Tree. Police quickly arrived to get rid of the flowers, prompting mourners to create a virtual equivalent of the tree online - where hundreds of thousands of people have since sent tributes and paid respects.Pressurised by more than a year's worth of growing suspicion and a rush of online attention, the issue had become too big to ignore. Then, last Monday, the government made an extraordinary admission.State broadcaster Vietnam Television (VTV) televised an official statement from authorities, confirming what had happened on the day of the incident. Former National Assembly deputy Nguyen Sy Cuong was indeed driving his car down Nguyen Huy Tu Street on 30 May, 2025, when his vehicle suddenly swerved across the road and into an oncoming motorcycle.VTV cited police and prosecution sources who said that because Nguyen Sy Cuong "sincerely confessed and actively and fully remedied the consequences of his actions", Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's family had submitted a petition to exempt him from prosecution. The report did not specify what form this remedy took, but Nguyen Sy Cuong was cleared of all criminal liability.While such a decision is lawful under Vietnam's legislation, lawyers have questioned whether the criminal proceedings were conducted in accordance with due process – or conducted at all. Social media users were quick to highlight his political connections and call for a more thorough investigation.Such online pressure had yielded results in the past.In March this year, a 66-year-old man driving under the influence of alcohol in Hanoi collided with seven other cars and three motorcycles in a chain-reaction crash that killed one woman and seriously injured two others.In the wake of that incident, it emerged that the driver, Nguyen Van Sau, was a retired police colonel who had previously served as deputy director of a department under the Ministry of Public Security. Fearing that the driver was not being held culpable, the victim's family appealed for help. Social media users in turn amplified the issue, and after three months Nguyen Van Sau was charged with "violating regulations on participation in road traffic".Many now feel that a similar groundswell may be the only way to deliver justice for the teenager who died last year. But their efforts have been met with friction.Do Viet Hung, the teenager's father, appeared in VTV's broadcast to thank internet users for their sympathy, but said the family was satisfied with the investigation's findings, and asked people to leave them alone. Notably, he also warned people "not to be drawn into the influence of reactionary elements".Also appearing in the broadcast was a senior police official, who suggested that people were leveraging the incident to stoke dissent.The Ministry of Public Security had "uncovered highly dangerous plots and intentions by hostile forces, reactionaries and bad actors to incite unrest and cause disorder", the official said."The ministry advises the public, especially young people, to remain fully alert and highly vigilant."Similar rebukes have also started emerging on social media, with some claiming that conspiratorial forces were manipulating young people in Vietnam to stoke political discontent, manipulate public opinion online and rally people in real life ahead of the country's national holiday on 2 September.Others have accused Gen Z Vietnamese of plotting a "colour revolution" – a term used to refer to mostly nonviolent protest movements that use specific colours or flowers as their symbol.This is a familiar line of critique from Vietnamese authorities, who have previously labelled people's grievances or resentments as being untrue, unreasonable, or stemming from information fabricated by some "anti-government" or "reactionary" organisation.Many in this case have said such accusations are baseless, insisting they are simply seeking justice for the victim of a fatal traffic accident. But the growing outrage has inevitably become a flashpoint amid broader, simmering grievances felt by Vietnam's youth.Despite the Vietnamese government's tightening control over people's online freedom of expression – through measures ranging from intimidation and fines to criminal prosecution – public opinion in some corners has started to swerve against the Communist Party line.On platforms such as Threads and Reddit, where anonymity is more normalised, many young people have expressed discontent towards various social issues: from the expansion of police power and land reclamation projects to exam cheating scandals and stricter regulation of online communication.Such grievances echo those condemned by other Gen Z-led movements across the broader Asia region.In countries like Bangladesh, India and Nepal, youth-led anti-government uprisings have over the past 12 months rallied immense support against the various pressure points of corruption, nepotism, economic inequality and democratic backsliding. Unofficially dubbed "the Asian Spring", the expanding influence of these movements has spread from Iran, Mongolia and the Maldives to the Philippines and Timor-Leste.But protests in Vietnam have rarely, if ever, reached such fierce extremes. Vietnamese authorities have historically proven effective at detecting and stifling dissent before it boils over into action. Virtual places of mourning, anonymous social media posts, and online protests seem to be the most strident action many civilians here can afford to take.Many are simply seeking justice for a teenager who was killed in a tragic accident, and accountability for a former lawmaker who appears to have been granted special clemency.Yet even the mere suggestion that this incident could foment an uprising has provoked alarm – along with harsh reminders of the longstanding status quo in Vietnam's one-party state."Are these Gen Z kids planning a colour revolution using this accident?" reads one widely shared post. "Are they trying to emulate Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, and then create an Asian Spring? Remember, this is Vietnam! This is not Nepal, India, or Bangladesh!"

schema.headline: Vietnam: Gen Z seek justice for teen killed in ex-politician's car crash

title: Viral Cat in the Hat TikTok trend sparks fake videos and real fear
description: "He's so scary!" says 16-year-old Skye, recoiling at the mention of the Cat in the Hat.Viral images purporting to show a life-sized version of the Dr
body: "He's so scary!" says 16-year-old Skye, recoiling at the mention of the Cat in the Hat.Viral images purporting to show a life-sized version of the Dr Seuss character on the streets after dark have sparked fear and confusion among teenagers. The posts, seen by millions, have convinced some young people that the character is real and that they might encounter it, prompting police forces in Ireland and the UK to issue statements confirming that the images and videos are fake."I was having a sleepover," Skye elaborates, "but everyone started watching Cat in the Hat videos. It was 3am. I wanted to go home. When I started walking down my friends' driveway, I got totally freaked out that the Cat in the Hat was going to jump out. I had to call my mum to pick me up."A quick scroll through TikTok reveals numerous accounts, many of them created in the past few weeks, sharing photos and videos of an elusive black-and-white feline wearing the famous, towering, crooked red-and-white striped hat.One post showing the original Cat in the Hat costume, accompanied by the caption "Help, what do I do?", has received 14.6m views in just three weeks.The comments add to the sense of frenzy, with followers asking, "Why is he taxidermied?" Others zoom in on parts of the costume and post conspiracy theories about Mike Myers, who played the character in the 2003 film, being trapped inside.Another popular account set up this week, posts videos of a real person dressed in a cat in the hat costume, dancing, with captions like "Kent I'm coming. lock your doors." Other users are sharing the videos, adding their own captions and locations across the UK.Many of the AI generated images have been centred on the Irish counties of Limerick and Wexford, where shaky videos purportedly showed the character wandering through the streets, causing alarm and confusion among residents.In Wexford, the local Gardaí (police force) quickly dismissed the sightings as fake and confirmed that the images had been generated using artificial intelligence.That has not stopped the pictures and videos from spreading online - along with unverified claims posted without evidence that the Cat in the Hat has been involved in violent assaults."I low-key wanna go meet him…" says 14-year-old Lily, who heard that the Cat in the Hat had arranged a "meet and greet", inviting local TikTok followers to come to the woods in Galashiels, a small town in the Scottish Borders.Her mother was horrified by the prospect."You are not going to meet anyone in the woods in the middle of the night!" she told her.There is a point at which viral dancing videos and AI-generated clips of the Cat in the Hat become something potentially more sinister, with real-world consequences beyond their impact on teenage imaginations.In England, South Yorkshire Police has denied social media claims that a 'killer Cat in the Hat' has been spotted. Posts about the alleged sightings have attracted hundreds of thousands of views on TikTok.There is also a fake Facebook post claiming to be from Yorkshire Police - no force with that name actually exists - and suggesting that the force is taking the rumoured sighting seriously.In response, a South Yorkshire Police spokesperson said: "If you do see posts online providing policing updates and advice, please check that they are from an official policing account. The cat is not out of the hat on this one… Please don't believe everything you read on social media."As with so many trends driven by TikTok, comedic reaction and spoofery is what will be appearing right now on many people's For You page.In recent days, depending largely on what your algorithm serves up, you may be seeing nearly as many people in Cat in the Hat costumes dancing to Beyonce as those stalking the streets. There are several jokey videos depicting police chasing human sized cats, and Scottish drag performer Ellie Diamond has issued a video declaring that she is not the Cat in the Hat killer. And Irish TikTok star Garron Noone said on one post that it should have been obvious it was a hoax "because even the most soulless, evil, vicious monster" would be "traumatised looking in the window of a Wexford person".Snapchat filters and images shared in group chats suggest that many teenagers - and those not so young - are simply having harmless fun with the trend.But some do remain perturbed, including another teenager in the Scottish borders, 16-year-old Ellie, who says: "I was so scared of him when I was little," Ellie confides. "Now it's like he's actually come to life to haunt me."Emily, a mother in Scotland, says the trend reminds her of the "Momo Challenge", a notorious internet hoax and digital urban legend. At the time, fact-checkers and authorities found no verified evidence linking the meme to children harming themselves, although the frightening images were still capable of causing distress."I'm not worried about my daughters, but there could be people with bad intentions who might take advantage of this trend to manipulate teenagers."For now, the evidence points not to a real, roaming Cat in the Hat, but to a rapidly evolving online story built from an auctioned film costume, people in costume, AI-generated material and unverified posts.Whether the claims began as a joke or were deliberately designed to frighten and manipulate, the advice from police is the same: pause before sharing, check the original source and date, look for confirmation from official police accounts, and treat invitations to meet strangers, especially at night or in isolated places, as a serious warning sign.The rapidly evolving trend terrorising or tantalising teenagers on TikTok across the UK and Ireland is a reminder that online fear can quickly spill into the real world.Additional reporting by John Hand

schema.headline: Viral Cat in the Hat TikTok trend sparks fake videos and real fear

title: Trump waves green flag at IndyCar race through Washington DC
description: Image source, ReutersByKwasi Gyamfi Asiedu and Helena Humphrey Reporting fromat the IndyCar fan zone in Washington DCUS President Donald Trump was amo
body: Image source, ReutersByKwasi Gyamfi Asiedu and Helena Humphrey Reporting fromat the IndyCar fan zone in Washington DCUS President Donald Trump was among hundreds of people who gathered to see the IndyCar race through the streets of Washington DC on Sunday, marking the culmination of a series of summer events to celebrate the country's 250th birthday.Driver Kyle Kirkwood won the race, earning his seventh career Indycar win.Ahead of the race, the president and First Lady Melania Trump took a ceremonial lap of the 1.7-mile track in his presidential limousine, The Beast.As they reached the finish line, Trump's new Air Force One completed a flyover above the capital.The Freedom 250 Grand Prix is the first time professional road racing has been hosted in the capital.Image source, ReutersImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Melania Trump waved to fans from the trackImage source, ReutersFigure caption, What do locals think of IndyCar?With a maximum speed limit of 55mph (89km/h), Washington DC has the lowest speed limit in the United States. But on Sunday, some of the world's fastest drivers zoomed past the capital's famous monuments and museums at speeds of up to 190mph (306km/h).The 25 professional drivers competing in the event faced 147 laps featuring seven crucial turns, making a total 250-mile course - a nod to the nation's anniversary.The drivers sped past the Washington Monument and museums on the National Mall, before passing a finish line with the US Capitol building in frame.Figure caption, The BBC's Helena Humphrey took a test drive of the track earlier in the weekSimilar to Formula 1, the IndyCar series is a road race featuring open-wheel, single-seater cars.But unlike F1, in which teams design and build their own cars, the engines in IndyCars come exclusively from Chevrolet or Honda.Image source, ReutersOrganisers of the Freedom 250 Grand Prix say about 140,000 people are expected to attend, with many given free general admission tickets through a lottery.However, premium packages sold for $5,000 ($3,700) for a pair of passes.The event has been a huge logistical and security lift for the city, and has led to widespread road closures, manholes being bolted down, and road resurfacing.The Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, which primarily runs domestic flights, has been under a three-hour airspace closure to accommodate the US military flyover.Image source, Getty ImagesThe National Gallery of Art conducted vibration tests to ensure its priceless collection could withstand the powerful rumble of the engines.On race day, however, the roar of celebration appeared to largely drown out any irritation. Many of those lining the circuit were there after winning tickets through a public lottery. Some wore Uncle Sam hats, while one woman came dressed as the Statue of Liberty. Families had travelled from across the country for what they saw as a once-in-a-lifetime event.US driver Josef Newgarden told the BBC that the significance of racing through the capital was not lost on him."It's super unique. You might never see this again, and as an American driver, it's very special celebrating the 250th anniversary of the country," he said. "It's a beautiful city, and it's very surreal."In other events earlier this summer, Trump hosted an Ultimate Fighting Championship event on the White House lawn, as well as a fireworks show on 4 July.Image source, Getty ImagesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Driver David Malukas' car is carried out after crashingImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A pit stop for driver Felix Rosenqvist

schema.headline: Trump waves green flag at IndyCar race through Washington DC

title: Brydon Carse: What will it take to prevent England from more hangovers
description: Yet again, the England men's cricket team is picking through the wreckage of a late-night misdemeanour. The latest stain on the game's reputation is a
body: Yet again, the England men's cricket team is picking through the wreckage of a late-night misdemeanour. The latest stain on the game's reputation is a result of pictures of fast bowler Brydon Carse in handcuffs and surrounded by police officers outside a nightspot in Derby. His Durham team-mate Matthew Potts is in the images, while former England captain Ben Stokes appears in the background.If you're keeping score, we're now up to eight England players involved in incidents of this kind since Halloween last year.Harry Brook was punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington, with Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue present. Ben Duckett was filmed drunk in Noosa, then Stokes and Gus Atkinson were there when a member of England's security staff was struck in a London nightclub in June, breaching a curfew in the process.To put it another way, there are 30 men currently on England central contracts. More than a quarter of them have been caught up in bother in the past 10 months. Of the four separate incidents, two have involved punches being thrown and another was a police matter.In Carse's case, the time spent in handcuffs came days after new England Test captain Joe Root called on his players to be "really good role models, good human beings".Root was speaking the day before England's first Test against Pakistan, for which Carse was part of the squad. The match was scheduled to still be ongoing when he found himself in the hands of the police.It is understood that Carse was not arrested. Both the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) and the Cricket Regulator will work to establish what happened. There are early suggestions he was denied entry back into a nightclub, or he had a drink poured over him.Carse was also not specifically on England duty at the time. He was released from the first-Test squad to play for Durham away at Derbyshire and was scheduled to report to Lord's for the second Test on Monday.As of Sunday evening, he remains part of the squad for the second Test. England will take time to gather some information before a decision on his involvement is made.Root warned his squad to "be adults" when he abolished the midnight curfew - in his first act as captain - that came into place after previous incidents. As part of that move, guidelines advising players about not drinking alcohol on the day before, during or after a game, or in public, have also been removed.There is a duty of care towards Carse. Two years ago, the 31-year-old was banned for historical betting offences and rebuilt his career to become an England regular in all three formats. No bowler has more Test wickets for England than Carse's 58 since he made his debut in October 2024.But there is also a deep sense of anger and frustration within the ECB at having to deal with another error of judgement by a high-profile player. Supporters will take their own view, among them a sense that the behaviour of these players is now beyond parody.Does someone have to be left out of a squad or given a meaty suspension for the penny to drop? This might be the opportunity for Root to stamp his authority on a new era.Naturally, there will once again be the debate about not denying players their freedom or stopping them from enjoying a victory.For Carse, a Saturday night out came less than 48 hours before he is scheduled to report for England. He is only a tweaked hamstring away from playing in a Test at Lord's on Thursday.Perhaps more damning is the kind of trouble this group of England players seem to find. Two punch-ups and a set of handcuffs. It also does not appear to have dawned on them that they are high-profile individuals, likely to attract attention, with footage finding its way to social media, as happened with Carse.And what about Stokes, who, despite being retired, remains an employee of the ECB via his central contract.As the former captain, should Stokes have been conscious about Carse being in that situation? What about the trouble in which Atkinson found himself alongside Stokes in June?Three weeks ago, Stokes denied the England team has a drinking culture, but rather that the game itself has a problem. What has Stokes done to distance himself or those around him from that drinking culture?Now there is a wait to see what happens next. The ECB only became aware of the incident on Sunday afternoon. The governing body will take a breath overnight and decide if Carse needs to be removed from the Test squad.Perhaps, on Tuesday, director of cricket Rob Key will once again explain why the players he manages cannot keep themselves out of trouble. In the aftermath of the Stokes-Atkinson incident in June, Key denied that England have become a "national embarrassment". He may be asked again.Key also might be asked about the whereabouts of new Test coach Stephen Fleming, who does not take up his post until the winter. Might Carse have been less inclined to step out of line had the new sheriff been in town?Well, here is another situation for England to manage. Only strong action will ensure there are no more.

schema.headline: Brydon Carse: What will it take to prevent England from more hangovers

title: How easy is it to find an NHS dentist? It depends on where you live
description: Cornwall, Devon and Northamptonshire have seen some of the biggest reductions in the number of practices offering NHS care. In Cornwall, more than a q
body: Cornwall, Devon and Northamptonshire have seen some of the biggest reductions in the number of practices offering NHS care. In Cornwall, more than a quarter of practices that previously offered NHS treatment have stopped doing so, making it one of the starkest examples of the shift away from NHS dentistry.The findings come as ministers have pledged to tackle so-called "dental deserts", but dentists say the current deal is not viable. Many have handed back their NHS contracts because to work is loss-making.In Somerset, fewer than one in five dental practices now offers NHS services. Alan, 83, who lives in the county, says he has given up trying to find an NHS dentist."I used to try, but getting a dental appointment anywhere near where I live would be impossible," he says.Alan has only one tooth remaining after the others "crumbled out over the years" and says he has had to adapt what he eats, although he jokes that he has perfected a way of eating Brazil nuts.Vivak Shah, who runs three dental practices in Northamptonshire, continues to offer NHS treatment but says it operates at a loss. He no longer takes on new NHS patients."Each year we struggle to decide what to do, and there is a limit to how much the private side can cover the NHS losses," says Shah.He warned that if practices stop providing NHS treatment, many patients could be left in pain or forced to seek help elsewhere in the health service, including hospital accident and emergency departments."A contract handed back in one town attracts little national attention on its own but repeated across the country for a decade it amounts to the quiet transformation of dentistry into a two-tier service," says Mark Dayan, head of public affairs at the Nuffield Trust."Access to dental care increasingly depends on what people can afford to pay and where they live."Jim Sykes is a dentist in Hexham. He handed back his NHS contract in 2024."It was a really hard emotional decision, but the NHS work was running at such a loss. I had to think of my team of staff and make it work," he says. Sykes asked if he could continue treating just children but was told he had to accept adults as well, or give up the NHS work."There has been a real breakdown in trust for me. Even if there was a new government offer, I would still be very nervous about entering a new NHS contract," he says.Sykes says that none of his friends in his graduating class in dentistry still works in the NHS. "My friends have gone private, retired or teach - any pathway to avoid NHS dentistry."Shiv Pabary, chair of the British Dental Association's General Dental Practice Committee, says the situation is "the direct result of choices made by successive governments". He warns that unless ministers "fix and fund NHS dentistry", more dentists could choose to reduce their NHS work or leave the service altogether.Overall dentist practice numbers have risen in England over the last decade."This is not a shortage of dentistry but a shortage of NHS dentistry," says Dayan. "Practices will need to be incentivised back into NHS work in the places where the NHS footprint has thinned most."While most parts of England recorded declines in practices offering NHS dental care, the reductions were smallest in North West London, the Black Country and North East London.North East London was the only area to see any increase during the period, recording one additional practice offering NHS treatment compared with a decade ago.Every other region of England saw the number of NHS dental practices fall.Looking at the number of practices doing NHS work is not the same as looking at exactly how much health service capacity there is - practices can vary in size. But if you look at other measures such as the amount of treatment being done, the numbers are still down, although not as steep as the fall in practice numbers.The government says that it is changing the dental contract and training more dentists in the areas most in need. The government says it will also make it a requirement for newly qualified dentists to practice in the NHS for a minimum period of at least three years.Campaign group 38 degrees calls the current dental crisis "shameful", with people being "forced to pay money they can't afford or suffer with the pain, shame, and further complications that come from being denied vital NHS healthcare".

schema.headline: How easy is it to find an NHS dentist? It depends on where you live

title: Gianni Infantino: Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin rules himself out of Fifa presidency bid
description: Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin has ruled himself out of the running to replace Gianni Infantino, but says he expects a candidate to challenge the F
body: Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin has ruled himself out of the running to replace Gianni Infantino, but says he expects a candidate to challenge the Fifa president's leadership in March.Infantino has faced calls to step down after he scrapped a controversial plan to sell off stakes in Fifa's competitions to private investors following widespread opposition.Uefa led the backlash to the plan, with its members voting to boycott World Cups unless it was scrapped, while European football's governing body said it has lost confidence in Infantino.Ceferin, 57, has been widely seen as a potential challenger to Infantino, but says he does not plan to stand for the position at the Fifa Congress in March 2027."I'm not interested because of two reasons. One reason is that I love Uefa and I love working here, and I think that at a certain point, it's time to also enjoy life a bit," Ceferin said on the Rest is Politics podcast, external."The second point is, my credibility is much, much higher if I'm not interested in the position."Ceferin says he either expects 56-year-old Swiss Infantino to step down because of a lack of support, or to face a challenge to his role from another candidate."One option is that he realises that he doesn't have the support, and that's not only a political support of the ones who vote, but the political support of football community, the political support of fans, the political support of the players, former players, coaches," he said."And the second option that he goes to the elections in March, but in that case, I think he will have a candidate against him. I don't know yet who."Infantino's scrapped proposal involved creating a new company - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) - to manage the commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, with 21% to be sold off to a private investment company.A number of football associations have withdrawn their support for Infantino, who was accused of breaking trust "through deception" in an open letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation.The football associations of all the home nations have withdrawn support for Infantino, but he retains the support of South American governing body Conmebol and Caf, the African governing body.Infantino - who worked at Uefa for 16 years, and was general secretary for nine - has been flying around the world this month in the search of public support.On Saturday, he met with Caribbean Football Union members in the Dominican Republic and on Sunday he was at the E-Sports World Cup in Paris, attended by the French President Emmanuel Macron, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Portugal forward Cristiano Ronaldo.Ceferin said someone "should remind Infantino that he is European" and described his Fifa counterpart's scrapped plan as "worse than the Super League".The European Super League was a proposed breakaway league of 20 top European clubs as a rival to Uefa's Champions League, but the project fell apart days after its unveiling in April 2021 after widespread criticism.Ceferin said that Uefa had no prior knowledge of Infantino's plan to sell stakes in Fifa's competitions, and that he found out through the media while on holiday with his family."They [Fifa] play on, you know, '[how] arrogant Europe is against us: They have enough money, but I help the small and the poor'," said Ceferin."But I think someone should remind him that he is a European, and that he was supported by Uefa, which he forgot."He added: "I think this plan is even worse than the Super League. Super important clubs wanted to do their own league, which is wrong, and would destroy football. But in this case, football would be literally sold."I'm absolutely sure that the plan is dead. It's hard to to imagine what kind of people would sell the sport that belongs to everyone. We will not allow that to happen."Before his aborted FFE proposal, Infantino was coming under increasing pressure over his relationship with United States President Donald Trump.After US striker Folarin Balogun had a red card suspension overturned so that he could play in his side's defeat by Belgium in the last 16 of this summer's World Cup, Trump revealed he personally called Infantino to request the sanction be lifted.Earlier this month, Trump said it would be a "terrible mistake" to remove Infantino as Fifa president."That was more than shocking. We have rules, and if you don't respect your own rules, then the game doesn't make any sense," Ceferin said on the incident."The president of a country says: 'I called him, and I told him to look at it.' And then the Fifa president says it was an independent decision. "I mean, for us as football fans, or for us as a governing body, that's shocking. That's shocking, and - trust me - almost everybody was shocked. Just not everybody dared to speak."

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin rules himself out of Fifa presidency bid

title: Doctors wrongly said I was too young to have endometriosis at 13
description: But the most frustrating thing for Grace, and why she contacted BBC Your Voice, is because she does not feel medical experts recognise that teenagers
body: But the most frustrating thing for Grace, and why she contacted BBC Your Voice, is because she does not feel medical experts recognise that teenagers and adolescents can suffer from endometriosis.Grace's GP did not diagnose her condition and nor did the first consultant she saw privately.She says: "Even a specialist didn't believe me. And if a specialist won't listen to me, who will?" It was not until the family pushed for a second private opinion that she got a positive diagnosis.Endometriosis, which occurs when tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows outside it, can cause debilitating symptoms, such as pelvic pain, heavy periods and fatigue.  About 10% of women are affected by it, according to NHS data.This week BBC presenter Emma Barnett revealed she had to have a hysterectomy for her endometriosis - which she said she never wanted to have. It can develop at any age once periods begin - and it is a common misconception that only older women suffer from the condition, says the charity Endometriosis UK,Faye Farthing, a spokesperson for the charity, says the government, NHS and health practitioners need to improve menstrual health education for young people "if we are to ensure the next generation are not robbed of the future they deserve".The charity says it can take a long time to diagnose endometriosis - an average of nine years in older women. And in the early stages, for example with teenagers, it often doesn't show up on an ultrasound scan. However, new tests are being developed which will help spot the condition earlier.Getting pregnant can be more difficult - even aged 14, Grace says she has been warned it is likely to affect her fertility. She's been advised she may not be able to have children after the age of 30 because of damage to her reproductive organs. She feels rushed: "I have to have kids within the next 15 years, otherwise I might not be able to."Paediatric gynaecologist Dr Gail Busby says nearly 80% of adolescents will have painful periods, but clinicians should recognise when a patient's symptoms are not normal - like missing school, missing PE every month or not going out with friends. She says: "When you're in bed and your best friend is a hot water bottle - that's not normal."Grace's case, showing symptoms at the age of 13, is not unusual, says Dr Busby, who sees girls both younger and older than Grace at her clinics. As well as her NHS work, she has opened a private adolescent endometriosis clinic in Manchester.The impact of symptoms is not just physical. Girls like Grace are more likely to suffer with anxiety or depression because their pain affects what is an important time for educational, emotional and social development."We should enjoy adolescence," Dr Busby says, "but they can't do what they enjoy doing, what their peers are enjoying doing."There is a history of endometriosis in Grace's family, but her mum Samantha says that did not make it any easier to get a diagnosis."When your child's on the floor in pain, it's very clear it's not just a bad period. But professionals say 'Oh we'll just put you on the pill for six months and see see how we go.'"Grace has recently had a laparoscopy - keyhole surgery - to remove her endometriosis. She hopes the procedure will help relieve her symptoms, at least temporarily. She has been advised to take a hormonal contraceptive to help slow monthly tissue growth and lessen the pain.By speaking out, Grace hopes more teenagers will have the confidence to pursue a diagnosis. "I felt I was going crazy. That it was all in my head," she says. "But actually, you know your body best and your pain is real."Additional reporting by Alex Emery

schema.headline: Doctors wrongly said I was too young to have endometriosis at 13

title: Service resumes on CrossCountry trains after power outage
description: On Sunday, a range of personal experiences were shared by passengers.Andy Burton, from Worcester, was travelling back from Cromford to Worcester after
body: On Sunday, a range of personal experiences were shared by passengers.Andy Burton, from Worcester, was travelling back from Cromford to Worcester after spending the weekend away with family celebrating his sister's birthday, but only got as far as Derby before his journey came to a premature end.He was forced to stay the night in a budget hotel in the hope he could return home on Monday."It was only once I had arrived at Derby that a member of staff told me my planned alternative route via Leicester had also been cancelled, because it was part of the CrossCountry disruption," he said."I soon realised I was stranded, as they said there was no alternative train route back to Worcester."It's not the best end to a great weekend away."Reese Proctor described the cancellations as "frustrating and unacceptable" as he tried to get to Manchester's Etihad Stadium in time for a 14:00 BST kick-off against Bournemouth.He had hoped to get a train from Reading to Manchester, but instead resorted to driving more than 100 miles to his friend's house in Leicester before driving on to the stadium.The 22-year-old told BBC Newsbeat the drive had added an extra two hours to his journey, leaving him "fuming".

schema.headline: Service resumes on CrossCountry trains after power outage

title: Dutch Grand Prix: Lando Norris and McLaren 'don't have car' to fight for title
description: Lando Norris says he and McLaren "don't have the car I need to fight for a championship", despite a second consecutive win to open the second half of
body: Lando Norris says he and McLaren "don't have the car I need to fight for a championship", despite a second consecutive win to open the second half of the Formula 1 season.The Briton's victory in the final Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort, following on from his first win of the season in Hungary last month, was of the highest calibre. As such, it raises the prospect of the sort of championship fightback staged by Red Bull's Max Verstappen against Norris himself last year.After this race last year, Norris' team-mate Oscar Piastri had a 34-point advantage over the Briton and 104 over Verstappen. Yet Verstappen, after one of the all-time great fightbacks, finished the season just two points behind Norris as he won the title in Abu DhabiNorris' masterful victory in Zandvoort has left him 83 points off the lead, held by Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli, who he and McLaren passed on track after losing the lead at the chaotic start of the day.Antonelli's team-mate George Russell is tied on points with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, 59 behind the Italian.But while McLaren have made a major step forward with upgrades to their car that led to convincing wins in both Hungary and now the Netherlands, Norris believes that the car still has too many flaws to mount the sort of consistent attack Verstappen produced last year."I'm confident because we clearly have a strong car," he said. "We have a strong car in certain areas. It's not like last year where we were pretty good everywhere."We're very, very strong in high speed, and that's the place we've improved the car the most, is high-speed performance. No one matches us in high speed, and that's a good thing."My pace advantage to Mercedes in Turn Seven, Eight was crazy, but their advantage that they have to us in slow speed is also crazy."And therefore, I don't have the confidence to say, 'Yeah, I can easily fight for a championship for the rest of the season.'"I know I've just won two races in a row and had two poles in a row, but at the minute I don't have the car I need to fight for a championship. And I know that's quite a big comment."Norris' belief is based on his understanding that McLaren's slow-speed performance will be a handicap at the next race in Monza, and two races after that in Azerbaijan.Both tracks are dominated by long straights, which penalise the McLaren's high drag compared to Mercedes, and have very few high-speed corners where the car's strength can compensate for its weaknesses in slow turns.McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: “If we can confirm our improvements in Monza, then we can look with some optimism at the remainder of the season.”Norris' victory in Zandvoort, built around an off-set strategy and devastating pace once the cars were on the hard tyres in the second stint, underlined the level at which he is now operating.As impressive as Verstappen's revival was last year, Norris' own in the second half of the season was almost as good, as both made up ground on Piastri.And Norris believes he has built on the progress he made in his driving after a difficult start to 2025 to perform on an even higher plane in 2026."I was driving at a high level the second half of last year," he said. "It's tough to say, but I do think it's a trickier car to drive this year in some ways. And I think you can see that because the gaps between team-mates are often bigger this year, I would say, than it was last year."I do believe I'm able to understand situations better, to understand the car in a better way. It's still just horrible to drive, but I'm doing a better job at just understanding this, relaying this to my team, figuring stuff out."So, it's not just I'm driving better on track. I'm certainly eliminating my weaknesses on track, and I don't have so many, but it's also how I work off the track. And for me, yesterday to today is a perfect example of the work we put in overnight transformed our race and gave me the opportunity to win."Team principal Andrea Stella said he believed Norris was driving better than ever."Lando is driving and operating at a very high level," Stella said. "He's driving at the level of a world champion."What I like the most of his journey in Formula 1 is that he keeps improving."After the start of the 2025 season, something clicked, which is not only a single click, but it's a way of working with Lando, for Lando, and that we are adopting also on Oscar's side now in particular."This approach has led Lando to continuous improvements."It's almost like I see Lando stronger and stronger race by race. Because I think this weekend was nowhere near a weekend in which we could fight for the victory for granted, especially after having seen the performance in the sprint (in which Norris was passed by Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and finished third)."But we invested in trying to understand where was the opportunity from a tyre exploitation point of view and car improvement."And then when you have conditions in which the car slides in the race, there's not much grip, then I think he is the master in these kind of conditions."A couple of months ago, before the British Grand Prix, and before McLaren had won a race this season, Norris admitted in an interview with BBC Sport "a little bit" of frustration at not being able to defend the title he won last year.So it's perhaps no surprise that now he appears to have at least an outside chance of making a fist of it, he is not making any presumptions."One race at a time," he said. "I know a lot of people say it now, but it's the truth of it. There's no point thinking that far ahead."Obviously, two great weekends, but there's still plenty of things we can do better, and we need to do better if we want to fight for a championship."It's still harder than I would like, and I don't want a bigger gap, so we have to keep working hard. There's still plenty of races, plenty of opportunity for everyone. So, keep my head down, keep working, and they'll keep coming."McLaren's progress has come in the context of stagnation at Mercedes, whose lack of an upgrade to their car since Canada in May has led to them being caught by McLaren and Ferrari, a situation that has raised eyebrows among rival teams.The next Mercedes upgrade is not due until the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia in four races' time.For Antonelli - who also faces a grid penalty at his home race in Italy next time out because he needs to take a new engine that exceeds his allowance as a consequence of early-season reliability problems - it cannot come soon enough."Now as a team we need to find a little bit of time because McLaren have done a huge step," he said."So for sure, in this race, it's going to be more difficult, it's going to be challenging, but we're ready to do our best and to maximise every opportunity."And then hopefully it's going to be our turn to bring the package that's going to give us a little bit of the upper hand again."

schema.headline: Dutch Grand Prix: Lando Norris and McLaren 'don't have car' to fight for title

title: PCs killed in wrong-way A66 crash were heroes, say families
description: Two police officers who died when a car travelling the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle have been hailed as heroes by thei
body: Two police officers who died when a car travelling the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle have been hailed as heroes by their families.PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 near Middlesbrough on Saturday.The Passat's occupants - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.In tributes released by Cleveland Police, PC Clough's family said he had been "willing to help anyone", while PC Blades' wife described him as "loved beyond words"."No words will ever feel like the right words to honour our Matt," she said, adding that he had been a "beloved husband" and the "most devoted father" to their two young sons who would grow up knowing what an "incredible" dad he had been. "He gave his life in the line of duty, protecting and serving others with courage, dedication and selflessness," she said."The pain of losing him is beyond words, and our lives will never be the same."Neither will the love he gave us ever fade."He may have left this world committed to the duty he believed in, but his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave to his family."She ended the tribute to her husband: "Forever loved. Forever missed. Forever our superhero. Our Matt and Dad."PC Clough's family said he had had a "fantastic sense of humour", jumping "into action whenever needed". They added that he had been their "hero", always "willing to help anyone for any reason".They also said he had "proudly fought for his country to make the world a better place" and had always been "on public duty throughout his short life".In other tributes, a man who had known PC Clough posted on social media that he had been a "true friend, fantastic soldier and I have no doubt even better police officer".Seaton Carew FC, where PC Blades had recently become a coach and was preparing for his first season with its under-sevens team, said the officer and his family were "much loved members" of the club.FC Hartlepool, where PC Blades had coached the under-10s team, said he had been a "role model, mentor [and] friend" whom the children had "looked up to and admired"."His kindness, patience, and infectious personality made him loved by all who had the privilege of knowing him," the club added.Carmel College in Darlington, where PC Blades taught English before joining the police, remembered him as an "intelligent, kind and approachable teacher" who "gave generously of himself to the young people in his care".By Monday morning, more than £264,000 had been pledged for the officers' families in an online fundraiser set up by Cleveland Police Federation.It said the two officers had "paid the ultimate sacrifice in the line of duty"."They leave behind heartbroken loved ones who will struggle to come to terms with the loss of their loved one," the federation said, adding the organisation would support the families "at this unfathomable moment" with the money to be used "as they so wish". Earlier a group of police officers laid floral tributes at the police cordon on Eston Road.Some removed their hats and bowed their heads and took a brief moment of silence to remember their colleagues.They spoke briefly to other officers at the scene before leaving, with some hugging each other as they walked away.When someone dies following police contact, it is mandatory for the case to be referred to the IOPC.Its director of engagement, Derrick Campbell, said the watchdog recognised the "devastating impact" the crash had on Cleveland Police and the "wider policing community".He said: "We have obtained initial accounts of officers involved in the pursuit, the incident log and in-car footage of the incident."Work is ongoing to obtain additional material."IOPC investigators will continue to review and analyse all the evidence available to us."A video posted on a TikTok account believed to belong to Makai Saddington in March 2025 showed him and four other young people involved in what appears to be a police pursuit. The video has since been deleted.BBC Verify analysed the one minute 34 second-long clip, which showed the car driving on footpaths and parkland in Ormesby, Middlesbrough, with Saddington a rear-seat passenger.Another video posted by the same account, also since deleted, appears to show a joyride where a passenger is smoking, with the speedometer showing 100mph.Then, later in the video, a different car is set on fire. The passengers in this video are not identifiable.The government told TikTok and other social media companies to take down content featuring a social media trend showing people driving the wrong way down roads.Defence minister Luke Pollard told BBC Radio 5 Live: "We've communicated to those social media platforms that have been hosting content that celebrates this type of dangerous behaviour on our roads to take down that content."I think we all need to give the police time, but there's also things we can be doing in the meantime to make sure that the internet is a safer place for everyone, that doesn't celebrate and load views and therefore financial incentives on people to generate such awful content."Pollard said he wanted social media companies to "step up"."It's one of the reasons they've argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves," he said. "Well this is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it."Redcar and Cleveland Borough Council said the section of A66 in South Bank between Eston Road and Normanby Road would remain closed until later on Monday while repairs were carried out on the carriageway.

schema.headline: PCs killed in wrong-way A66 crash were heroes, say families
